Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

This paper investigates the many-to-one throughput capacity (and by symmetry, one-to-many throughput capacity) of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks. It has generally been assumed in prior studies that the many-to-one throughput capacity is upper-bounded by the link capacity L. Throughput capacity L is not achievable under 802.11. This paper introduces the notion of "canonical networks", which is a class of regularly-structured networks whose capacities can be analyzed more easily than unstructured networks. We show that the throughput capacity of canonical networks under 802.11 has an analytical upper bound of 3L/4 when the source nodes are two or more hops away from the sink; and simulated throughputs of 0.690L (0.740L) when the source nodes are many hops away. We conjecture that 3L/4 is also the upper bound for general networks. When all links have equal length, 2L/3 can be shown to be the upper bound for general networks. Our simulations show that 802.11 networks with random topologies operated with AODV routing can only achieve throughputs far below the upper bounds. Fortunately, by properly selecting routes near the gateway (or by properly positioning the relay nodes leading to the gateway) to fashion after the structure of canonical networks, the throughput can be improved significantly by more than 150%. Indeed, in a dense network, it is worthwhile to deactivate some of the relay nodes near the sink judiciously.

This study examines the many-to-one throughput capacity of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks, as well as the corresponding one-to-many capacity by symmetry. Earlier work has commonly treated the link capacity, denoted by L, as an upper limit for many-to-one throughput capacity. However, a throughput of L cannot actually be attained with 802.11.

The paper proposes the concept of “canonical networks,” a category of networks with regular structures that make capacity analysis simpler than in irregular network layouts. For these canonical networks under 802.11, the authors demonstrate an analytical upper bound of 3L/4 on throughput capacity when source nodes are at least two hops from the sink. Simulations further show achievable throughputs of 0.690L, or 0.740L in another case, when the source nodes are located many hops away.

The authors also conjecture that 3L/4 serves as the upper bound for general networks. In the special case where every link has the same length, they prove that 2L/3 is an upper bound for general networks. Their simulations indicate that randomly organized 802.11 networks using AODV routing obtain throughput levels much lower than these theoretical limits.

Nevertheless, throughput can be increased substantially—by more than 150%—if routes near the gateway are chosen appropriately, or if relay nodes leading to the gateway are positioned carefully, so that the resulting structure resembles that of canonical networks. In fact, for dense networks, selectively turning off some relay nodes close to the sink can be beneficial.

The paper investigates the throughput capacity of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks, focusing on two common traffic patterns: many-to-one and one-to-many communication. These patterns are especially important in practical wireless networks, such as sensor networks, mesh networks, and access networks, where many nodes may send data toward a single gateway or receive data from it.

A central argument of the paper is that the often-assumed upper bound of link capacity, denoted by \(L\), is not actually achievable in IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks. Although \(L\) may represent the nominal capacity of a single wireless link, real multi-hop operation introduces contention, interference, and medium-access constraints. As a result, the aggregate throughput that can be sustained near a gateway or sink is lower than this theoretical link capacity.

To make the capacity analysis more tractable, the authors introduce the concept of “canonical networks.” These are regular and structured network topologies designed to capture the essential behavior of multi-hop IEEE 802.11 networks while avoiding the complexity of arbitrary node placement. By studying these canonical networks, the authors are able to derive clearer analytical results about throughput limitations and bottlenecks.

For canonical networks operating under IEEE 802.11, the paper establishes an analytical upper bound on throughput capacity of \(3L/4\), provided that the source nodes are at least two hops away from the sink. This result shows that even under idealized and regular network conditions, the full link capacity \(L\) cannot be reached. The reduction is caused by the way IEEE 802.11 manages access to the shared wireless medium, particularly around heavily used nodes such as sinks or gateways.

The paper also presents simulation results showing that network performance can be significantly improved through careful routing and topology design. In particular, selecting appropriate routes or strategically positioning relay nodes near the gateway can increase throughput by more than 150%. These findings highlight that while IEEE 802.11 imposes fundamental capacity limits, intelligent network planning can substantially reduce bottlenecks and improve overall performance.

This paper investigates the throughput capacity of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop wireless networks, focusing on two important traffic patterns: many-to-one communication, where many nodes send data toward a single gateway or sink, and one-to-many communication, where a gateway distributes data to many nodes. These traffic patterns are common in wireless mesh networks, sensor networks, and community access networks, yet their achievable throughput is often lower than what would be predicted by simple link-capacity arguments.

To make the problem analytically manageable, the paper introduces a class of simplified but representative network models called “canonical networks.” These canonical networks capture the essential contention, interference, and forwarding behavior of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop systems while remaining tractable enough to derive capacity bounds. By studying these models, the authors show that the overall network throughput is not simply limited by the raw capacity of the bottleneck wireless link. Instead, the carrier-sensing and medium-access behavior of IEEE 802.11 imposes additional constraints, especially near the gateway where multiple flows converge or diverge.

A key result is that the throughput capacity of the canonical networks is bounded by \(3L/4\), where \(L\) denotes the effective single-link capacity. This is significantly below the traditional assumption that the maximum throughput should be close to \(L\). The result demonstrates that even under idealized and carefully structured conditions, IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks suffer from inherent capacity loss caused by contention among neighboring transmitters and relays.

The paper then compares these analytical bounds with simulation results and with more realistic network scenarios. In practical random topologies using AODV routing, throughput is found to be much worse than the canonical-network bound. This degradation occurs because random node placement and conventional shortest-path routing tend to create severe congestion near the gateway. Many routes funnel through a small number of relay nodes, producing contention hotspots and reducing the amount of traffic the network can successfully carry.

However, the paper also shows that performance can be substantially improved through better topology and routing design. By carefully shaping routes so that traffic is more evenly distributed, or by strategically placing relay nodes near the gateway, the network can avoid excessive concentration of load on a few bottleneck nodes. These strategies significantly reduce contention and improve spatial reuse. In some cases, such improvements increase throughput by more than 150% compared with unoptimized random AODV networks.

Overall, the paper argues that the capacity of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks must be understood in terms of MAC-layer contention, routing structure, and node placement, rather than simple link-rate assumptions. The canonical-network analysis provides useful theoretical bounds, while the simulations show that practical performance depends heavily on how traffic is routed and how relays are arranged around the gateway. The findings suggest that substantial throughput gains are possible, but only if network design explicitly accounts for the bottlenecks created by many-to-one and one-to-many traffic patterns.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the abstract of a paper about many-to-one throughput capacity in IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks, including its main results, upper bounds, simulations, and practical implications.
counterfactuals.output:
The paper studies the **many-to-one throughput capacity** of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop wireless networks, where many nodes send traffic toward a single sink or gateway — a common pattern in sensor networks, mesh networks, and community Wi-Fi backhaul systems.

Its main message is that **the throughput of such networks is fundamentally limited by the bottleneck around the destination**, rather than by the average capacity of the whole network.

Key points:

- **Main result:** In an IEEE 802.11 multi-hop network with many sources sending to one receiver, the total sustainable throughput is constrained by the ability of the nodes near the sink to forward traffic. As the number of nodes grows, the per-source throughput decreases sharply, typically on the order of \(1/n\), because all flows eventually contend for the same local wireless resources near the destination.

- **Upper bounds:** The paper derives analytical upper bounds on achievable throughput. These bounds account for interference, carrier sensing, MAC-layer contention, and the fact that packets from many flows must pass through a small number of relay nodes close to the sink. The results show that even with ideal routing, the many-to-one traffic pattern creates a capacity bottleneck that cannot be avoided by simply adding more nodes.

- **Simulation results:** Simulations of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks support the theoretical analysis. They show that measured throughput approaches the predicted limits and that performance degradation is mainly caused by congestion and contention near the sink. The simulations also illustrate that nodes closer to the destination carry disproportionate relay load and therefore determine the network’s overall capacity.

- **Practical implications:** The work suggests that large 802.11 multi-hop networks are poorly suited to heavy many-to-one traffic unless the bottleneck near the sink is addressed. Practical improvements may require multiple gateways, traffic balancing, careful sink placement, channel assignment, directional antennas, rate control, or MAC/routing protocols designed specifically for convergecast traffic. Simply increasing network density or adding more relay nodes does not necessarily improve throughput and may even worsen contention.

Overall, the abstract emphasizes that **many-to-one communication in IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks has a severe structural capacity limit**, and that network design must focus on relieving congestion around the sink to achieve scalable performance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a concise academic abstract for a research paper investigating why IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks cannot achieve link capacity L in many-to-one traffic scenarios and how canonical network structures improve throughput.
counterfactuals.output:
This paper investigates the throughput limitations of IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks under many-to-one traffic, a common pattern in sensor, mesh, and access networks where multiple sources forward data toward a single sink. Although each wireless link has nominal capacity \(L\), we show that aggregate forwarding constraints, medium contention, interference, and relay bottlenecks prevent flows near the sink from achieving \(L\). In particular, nodes closer to the destination must carry both locally generated and transit traffic while competing for the same shared channel, causing severe spatial unfairness and capacity collapse. We analyze how these effects arise from the interaction between carrier sensing, collision avoidance, and multi-hop forwarding, and demonstrate that the achievable throughput is governed not by individual link capacity but by contention domains and traffic concentration.

The paper further examines canonical network structures that reorganize forwarding paths and contention relationships to improve throughput. By reducing redundant contention, balancing relay loads, and increasing spatial reuse, these structures provide a more efficient use of the wireless medium and mitigate bottlenecks near the sink. Analytical arguments and comparative evaluation show that canonical topologies can substantially increase stable aggregate throughput relative to unstructured multi-hop routing. The results clarify why link-level capacity is an insufficient predictor of network performance and highlight the importance of topology-aware design for scalable IEEE 802.11 many-to-one networks.

The study’s key contributions can be summarized as follows:

- **Canonical multi-hop network models:**  
  The work introduces or analyzes simplified “canonical” IEEE 802.11 multi-hop network topologies. These canonical networks are used to isolate the fundamental capacity behavior of 802.11 forwarding without the extra complexity of arbitrary node placement, routing instability, or traffic heterogeneity.

- **Theoretical capacity bound of \(3L/4\):**  
  A major result is the derivation of an upper bound on achievable network throughput. If \(L\) denotes the capacity of a single IEEE 802.11 link, then the study shows that the maximum sustainable throughput in the considered multi-hop setting is bounded by approximately  
  \[
  \frac{3L}{4}.
  \]
  This bound reflects the fact that forwarding traffic over multiple wireless hops consumes shared channel resources and creates contention among neighboring transmitters.

- **Simulation results close to the bound:**  
  Simulations of the canonical networks show aggregate throughput values around  
  \[
  0.690L \text{ to } 0.740L,
  \]
  depending on topology and configuration. These results are close to the theoretical \(3L/4 = 0.750L\) limit, suggesting that the analytical bound is meaningful and that IEEE 802.11 can approach it under controlled, well-structured conditions.

- **Comparison with random AODV-based topologies:**  
  The study also compares the canonical results with more realistic random multi-hop topologies using AODV routing. In these random networks, performance is generally lower and more variable because routes are not necessarily capacity-efficient, contention patterns are irregular, and traffic can concentrate around bottleneck nodes.

- **Route optimization near gateways:**  
  A key observation is that performance in random or infrastructure-connected multi-hop networks is often limited by congestion near gateways or sink nodes. The study highlights that optimizing routes near these gateways—rather than only finding shortest paths—can significantly improve throughput by balancing load and reducing local contention.

Overall, the contribution is to connect a clean theoretical capacity result, \(3L/4\), with simulation evidence showing practical throughput near \(0.690L\)–\(0.740L\), and to demonstrate that routing choices, especially around gateways, are critical in real IEEE 802.11 multi-hop network performance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a technical summary of research findings on many-to-one and one-to-many throughput capacity in 802.11 networks, emphasizing analytical capacity bounds, equal-link-length cases, and the benefit of deactivating relay nodes near the sink.
counterfactuals.output:
## Technical summary: many-to-one and one-to-many capacity in 802.11 multi-hop networks

Research on 802.11 multi-hop throughput capacity shows that **traffic pattern matters as much as node density or nominal PHY rate**. In particular, **many-to-one** traffic, such as sensor-to-sink collection, and **one-to-many** traffic, such as sink-to-actuator dissemination, create severe bottlenecks near the sink or source. Unlike random unicast traffic, where load is spatially spread, convergecast and multicast/broadcast-style traffic concentrate forwarding demand on a small set of relay links.

The main findings can be summarized as follows.

---

### 1. Many-to-one capacity is bottleneck-limited near the sink

In a many-to-one 802.11 network, all flows eventually cross a small region around the sink. Even if nodes far from the sink can reuse the channel spatially, the final few hops into the sink form a **contention and forwarding bottleneck**.

A typical analytical model represents each wireless link as consuming airtime and interfering with nearby links. If link \(i\) has capacity \(C_i\), forwarding load \(L_i\), and source injection rate \(\lambda\), then a basic feasibility condition is

\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} \frac{\lambda L_i}{C_i} \leq 1
\]

for every conflict set, clique, or carrier-sense region \(\mathcal{K}\). Thus,

\[
\lambda \leq 
\min_{\mathcal{K}}
\frac{1}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} L_i/C_i}.
\]

For equal-rate links with capacity \(C\),

\[
\lambda \leq 
\min_{\mathcal{K}}
\frac{C}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} L_i}.
\]

The dominant constraint is usually the one involving the links closest to the sink, because those links carry traffic from many upstream sources.

---

### 2. Aggregate capacity remains \(O(1)\); per-node capacity falls as \(O(1/N)\)

For a network with \(N\) sources sending to one sink, the aggregate offered rate is approximately \(N\lambda\). Because the sink region has only a constant amount of wireless airtime, the aggregate throughput does not scale linearly with \(N\). Instead,

\[
N\lambda = O(1),
\]

so the sustainable per-source rate behaves like

\[
\lambda = O\left(\frac{1}{N}\right).
\]

This is a stronger bottleneck than in some random unicast settings because all routes converge at one point. Adding more nodes does not increase sink capacity unless it also adds additional orthogonal channels, directional antennas, additional sinks, or other mechanisms that expand the bottleneck resource.

---

### 3. One-to-many traffic has a similar bottleneck by traffic reversal

One-to-many dissemination from a single source to many receivers exhibits an analogous bottleneck near the source. The source or its first-hop relays must inject all downstream traffic into the network.

Under symmetric links, identical PHY rates, and unicast forwarding, the capacity bounds for one-to-many are often comparable to those for many-to-one after reversing the routes. In both cases, a small neighborhood around the root node—the sink in convergecast or the source in dissemination—dominates the capacity.

However, one-to-many can differ in practice if the MAC uses broadcast, multicast, network coding, or opportunistic overhearing. With pure 802.11 unicast forwarding, the same airtime and interference constraints largely apply.

---

### 4. Equal-link-length cases yield clearer closed-form bounds

A common analytical simplification assumes that all links have the same length \(d\), the same PHY rate \(C\), and the same interference or carrier-sense radius. This produces simple capacity expressions because each link conflicts with a fixed number of neighboring links.

For example, in a line network with nodes forwarding toward a sink, suppose each link interferes with approximately \(q-1\) neighboring links, so a conflict region contains about \(q\) consecutive links. If link \(i\) carries \(L_i\) flows, then the per-source rate satisfies

\[
\lambda \leq 
\frac{C}{\max_{\mathcal{K}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} L_i}.
\]

Near the sink, the forwarding loads are largest. In a line with \(N\) sources, the last hop may carry \(N\) flows, the preceding hop \(N-1\), and so on. A bottleneck clique of \(q\) links near the sink carries total load approximately

\[
N + (N-1) + \cdots + (N-q+1)
= qN - \frac{q(q-1)}{2}.
\]

Thus,

\[
\lambda \lesssim 
\frac{C}{
qN - q(q-1)/2
},
\]

and the aggregate throughput satisfies

\[
N\lambda \lesssim \frac{C}{q}
\]

for large \(N\).

This illustrates the key equal-link-length result: **the interference span \(q\)** directly reduces the usable many-to-one aggregate capacity. Even with perfect scheduling, only a fraction of the nominal link rate can be converted into sink throughput because several heavily loaded links near the sink cannot be active simultaneously.

---

### 5. 802.11 contention makes the practical throughput lower than ideal schedule bounds

The analytical upper bounds are often derived from conflict-graph, protocol-model, or airtime-clique arguments. These bounds assume efficient scheduling. Real 802.11 CSMA/CA usually performs worse because of:

- contention overhead,
- backoff time,
- collisions,
- hidden terminals,
- exposed terminals,
- ACK overhead,
- unfairness between upstream and downstream relays,
- queue overflow near the sink,
- MAC-layer starvation of heavily loaded relays.

Therefore, the analytical capacity is typically an optimistic bound. Simulations and experiments generally show the same qualitative behavior—sink-region bottlenecking—but with lower numerical throughput.

---

### 6. Relay nodes near the sink can hurt rather than help

A counterintuitive finding is that activating every possible relay near the sink is not always beneficial. In dense 802.11 networks, nodes close to the sink may:

1. contend directly with the sink’s immediate relays,
2. increase carrier-sense blocking,
3. create additional short hops that consume airtime,
4. enlarge the local conflict region,
5. introduce extra forwarding transmissions without increasing the sink’s receive capacity.

Because all traffic must ultimately enter the sink through a limited number of last-hop transmissions, adding many relays near the sink can increase contention more than it increases spatial reuse.

As a result, **deactivating some relay nodes near the sink can increase aggregate throughput**.

---

### 7. Why deactivating near-sink relays improves capacity

The benefit comes from reducing the load in the most constrained conflict sets. If many short hops exist near the sink, a packet may require several transmissions inside the bottleneck region before reaching the sink. Each of those transmissions consumes airtime in a region where spatial reuse is already poor.

By forcing packets to use longer hops into the sink region, or by selecting only a small subset of near-sink relays, the network can reduce the number of transmissions competing in the dominant clique.

Conceptually, if the bottleneck constraint is

\[
\lambda \leq 
\frac{C}{\sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}_{sink}} L_i},
\]

then deactivating relays near the sink can reduce

\[
\sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}_{sink}} L_i,
\]

even if some individual hops become longer or slightly lower-rate. Throughput improves when the airtime saved by reducing local relaying and contention exceeds the airtime cost of using longer hops.

---

### 8. The optimal design often creates an inactive region around the sink

Several analytical and simulation studies find that the best routing/activation pattern may leave a region around the sink partially inactive, except for a carefully chosen set of gateway relays. This resembles a **relay-free zone** or **controlled access region**.

The intuition is:

- nodes very close to the sink do not provide much spatial reuse benefit;
- their transmissions are likely to conflict with the final hop into the sink;
- using too many of them fragments the path into many short, mutually interfering hops;
- a smaller number of well-positioned relays can aggregate traffic more efficiently.

Thus, near the sink, the objective is not maximum connectivity but minimum airtime consumption in the bottleneck area.

---

### 9. Equal-link-length results clarify when deactivation helps

In equal-link-length models, every additional hop near the sink consumes roughly the same airtime and conflicts with roughly the same number of neighboring hops. Therefore, the cost of extra relays is easy to see: each added relay layer near the sink adds another heavily loaded link to the dominant interference set.

If a bottleneck clique contains \(q\) links, and deactivating relays reduces the number of heavily loaded links inside that clique, the bound improves approximately in proportion to the reduction in total clique load.

For example, replacing several short hops near the sink with fewer longer hops can reduce the denominator in

\[
\lambda \leq 
\frac{C}{\max_{\mathcal{K}} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{K}} L_i}.
\]

The improvement is largest when the removed relays were carrying many flows and were located inside the sink’s carrier-sense or interference region.

---

### 10. Main capacity-design implications

The research leads to several practical conclusions for 802.11 many-to-one and one-to-many networks:

1. **The sink/source neighborhood determines capacity.**  
   Far-away spatial reuse matters less than the bottleneck near the traffic root.

2. **Per-node convergecast throughput decreases roughly as \(1/N\).**  
   More sources mean more sharing of the same final-hop airtime.

3. **Equal-link-length networks expose simple airtime bounds.**  
   Capacity is governed by the number of mutually interfering high-load links near the sink.

4. **Shortest-path routing is not always capacity-optimal.**  
   Shortest paths can create too many relay transmissions in the bottleneck region.

5. **Relay suppression near the sink can improve throughput.**  
   Selectively deactivating nodes reduces contention and airtime demand where the network is most constrained.

6. **A small set of designated relays or gateways is preferable to uncontrolled dense relaying.**

7. **Capacity gains require bottleneck expansion.**  
   Major improvements usually require multiple channels, multiple sinks, directional antennas, TDMA scheduling, rate-aware routing, or load-balanced sink placement.

In short, 802.11 many-to-one and one-to-many capacity is not primarily limited by the total number of nodes, but by the amount of airtime available in the high-load interference region around the sink or source. Analytical bounds based on conflict sets and equal-link-length assumptions show that this bottleneck imposes a constant aggregate capacity, and that deactivating near-sink relays can improve throughput by reducing unnecessary contention and forwarding load in the critical region.

counterfactuals.output: **Abstract—** Many-to-one traffic patterns are central to IEEE 802.11 multi-hop networks such as sensor, mesh, and community networks, where multiple sources deliver data to a single gateway. A common assumption is that the achievable many-to-one throughput is fundamentally bounded by the network radius or path length \(L\), due to forwarding load and contention near the sink. This paper challenges that assumption by showing that the \(L\)-based bound is not intrinsic to 802.11 multi-hop operation, but rather a consequence of particular topologies, routing structures, and contention patterns. We introduce the notion of **canonical networks**, a class of structured multi-hop topologies that exposes the relationship between carrier sensing, spatial reuse, routing, and bottleneck formation in many-to-one communication. Using this framework, we derive theoretical throughput bounds demonstrating that substantially higher many-to-one throughput is achievable than predicted by the conventional \(L\)-limited model. We further validate the analysis through packet-level simulations of IEEE 802.11 networks, showing that appropriate canonical constructions and routing choices can significantly improve aggregate sink throughput by increasing spatial reuse and reducing contention-induced serialization. The results indicate that many-to-one throughput in multi-hop 802.11 networks is not universally constrained by \(L\), and that topology-aware design can yield both analytically provable and practically observable performance gains.
